account:
Today is day 1, just after noon. I read my appointments this morning, attended office hours, inspected the mill's sale stock at ten, and returned home for lunch. The mill chest held 98 hay bales and 60 emeralds; I did not obtain a clear report on milling operations. I am due at the office at thirteen for council letters, at my neighbour's dockside cottage at fifteen for tea, and back at the office at sixteen-thirty. The innkeeper will meet me there at seventeen forty-five before our eighteen hundred great-hall meeting about the inn's service to town.

The unusual news is repeated, poorly explained talk of a bridge or port change at the bakery. Townsfolk 01 and 21 named the baker, innkeeper, and someone called freight as having been there, but supplied no concrete description. These accounts could be repetitions of the same rumour rather than independent observations. My neighbour personally crossed the bridge without trouble and explicitly called the change story unconfirmed. I therefore do not know whether anything actually changed, who arranged it, or its purpose. It might concern transport or deliveries, but that is only a possibility, not an established fact.

My neighbour also reported that the innkeeper described a quiet morning at the inn and spoke warmly of welcoming service. That fits the stated subject of our scheduled meeting, but I have no evidence connecting it to the bridge rumours. The secretary reported no new correspondence this morning. My next priority is to keep the council-letter appointment; when possible, I should ask the baker or innkeeper directly for specific firsthand details rather than spread the vague story.
